faq.q: Why use PEF instead of spirometry in low‑resource settings?

exam: A 25‑year‑old with wheeze presents in a rural clinic; you have only a peak flow meter – what is your immediate assessment and why? — Record a PEF, compare to personal best, and decide if the attack is mild, moderate or severe to guide bronchodilator dosing.

During an asthma review the patient’s diary shows a 25 % drop in evening PEF over the past week – what does this indicate and what step‑wise change should you consider? — Indicates loss of control; step up inhaled corticosteroid or add a long‑acting β2‑agonist.

A child with known asthma has a PEF of 45 % predicted after salbutamol – what red‑flag features would make you call for urgent transfer? — Persistent PEF < 50 % with tachypnoea, SpO₂ < 92 %, silent chest or altered mental status.

Explain why a patient with COPD may have a lower PEF than a similarly aged asthmatic, even when symptoms are similar. — COPD causes fixed airway narrowing and loss of elastic recoil, reducing maximal flow more than reversible asthma.

You suspect a severe asthma attack but the peak flow meter is broken; how do you proceed? — Rely on clinical signs (wheeze, work of breathing, SpO₂) and give immediate bronchodilator and oxygen while arranging transfer.

What is the rationale for avoiding high‑dose inhaled steroids during an acute severe attack? — They have delayed onset; systemic steroids act faster and avoid the risk of aerosol‑induced bronchospasm.

A patient reports using a peak flow meter daily but values are unchanged; what common error could explain this? — Submaximal effort or incorrect technique; re‑teach the patient and verify meter calibration.

How does biomass‑fuel exposure influence PEF trends in a rural adult? — Chronic irritant exposure leads to airway inflammation and fixed obstruction, causing progressively lower PEF readings over time.
ai.title: Peak Expiratory Flow
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Peak expiratory flow (PEF) measures the maximum speed of expiration and is a quick bedside tool for assessing large‑airway obstruction, especially asthma. It guides severity grading, treatment response and detection of diurnal variability.

b: Measured in litres per minute (L/min)
Requires patient to take a deep breath and blow forcefully into the device
Reference values are based on age, sex, height and ethnicity; personal best is the highest reproducible reading
sections.p: PEF is the highest flow (L/min) achieved during a forced exhalation from full lung inflation, recorded with a handheld peak flow meter. It is used to detect and monitor obstructive airway disease when spirometry is unavailable.

t.b: What is the current airway calibre? – Value <50 % predicted or personal best indicates severe obstruction; 50‑80 % suggests moderate disease

b: Mild: 80‑100 % predicted/personal best
Moderate: 50‑79 % predicted/personal best
Severe: <50 % predicted/personal best
sections.p: PEF percentages of predicted or personal best are used to stage asthma attacks and guide stepwise therapy.

t.b: Does the patient respond to a short‑acting β2‑agonist? – Increase ≥20 % indicates reversible obstruction

b: Asthma – most common, especially in children and young adults
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) – smokers, biomass‑fuel exposure
Acute severe bronchospasm – e.g., status asthmaticus, allergic reaction
Upper airway obstruction – foreign body, severe laryngeal edema (rare in low‑resource settings)
Post‑infectious airway narrowing – after severe pneumonia or TB
sections.p: Large‑airway obstruction that reduces expiratory flow is the primary mechanism.

b: Morning dip in PEF common in asthma
Rapid fall in PEF during an acute attack
Improvement after inhaled bronchodilator
sections.p: Patients with reduced PEF usually have wheeze, cough, chest tightness and variable dyspnoea. Diurnal variation (>20 % between morning and evening over 2 weeks) points to uncontrolled asthma.

b: Pulse oximetry – assesses oxygenation
Chest radiograph – rules out pneumonia, TB, pneumothorax
Spirometry – gold standard if available
sections.p: PEF is part of a broader assessment that may include clinical observation, pulse oximetry and, where possible, spirometry.

t.b: Is hypoxaemia present? – SpO₂ < 92 % warrants supplemental O₂ and urgent review
Is there an alternative cause for dyspnoea? – Hyperinflation supports obstructive disease; infiltrates suggest infection

b: PEF < 50 % predicted with rising respiratory rate
Silent chest or inability to speak full sentences
SpO₂ < 92 % despite oxygen
Altered consciousness
sections.p: Severe obstruction can progress to respiratory failure.

b: Short‑acting β2‑agonist (e.g., salbutamol) – first line for acute bronchodilation; rapid onset
Systemic corticosteroid (e.g., oral prednisolone) – reduces airway inflammation; avoid high‑dose inhaled steroids in severe attack
Oxygen therapy to maintain SpO₂ ≥ 92 % – nasal cannula preferred; avoid high‑flow mask if CO₂ retention risk
If infection suspected, give appropriate antibiotics (e.g., amoxicillin for bacterial pneumonia) – avoid unnecessary antibiotics in pure asthma
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, relieve bronchospasm, and monitor response with serial PEF.

b: Teach patient to keep a PEF diary; record morning and evening values
Review diary every 2 weeks; >20 % variation signals poor control
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus
Educate on avoidance of biomass smoke, tobacco, and occupational irritants
sections.p: Regular PEF monitoring helps detect loss of control early and guides step‑up or step‑down therapy.

b: FEV₁ measures volume expelled in the first second; PEF measures peak flow rate
Peak flow is effort‑dependent and less reproducible than spirometry
sections.p: PEF is sometimes mistaken for spirometric measures such as FEV₁.

b: Poor technique – submaximal effort gives falsely low values
Upper airway obstruction (e.g., severe nasal polyps) can lower PEF without lower‑airway disease
Very high values in children may be over‑estimated if the meter is not calibrated
sections.p: Factors that affect PEF accuracy must be recognised.

whenToSeekHelp: Silent chest or inability to speak full sentences
